title: Data Security Controls
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 2: Asset Security: Data Security Controls.

items: Scoping — Determining which parts of a standard/framework apply to your organization
Tailoring — Customizing selected controls to fit specific organizational needs
Baselines — Minimum security configuration levels for systems
Organizations may need compensating controls when standard controls aren't feasible
Control selection must balance security needs with business requirements

blocks.text: From Chapple: "Some controls aren't appropriate or feasible in a remote office location. In this situation, the organization can select compensating security controls to tailor the baseline to the remote location." Scoping narrows the list of controls to those relevant to the organization's environment. Tailoring adjusts those controls to fit specific needs while maintaining adequate security. Example: A NIST 800-53 control requires smart card authentication. If an organization cannot implement smart cards, they might tailor this control by implementing MFA with hardware tokens as a compensating control.

items: Network DLP — Scans files before they leave the network (including cloud DLP)
Endpoint DLP — Prevents users from copying, printing, or transferring sensitive files
Storage DLP — Scans data at rest for policy violations
DLP solutions use content inspection and contextual analysis
DLP relies on data classification to identify sensitive data

blocks.text: From Chapple: "Network DLP solutions scan files before they leave the network. Endpoint DLP solutions prevent users from copying or printing some files." DLP detection methods:

items: Keyword matching — Searching for specific terms
Pattern matching — Detecting data patterns (credit card numbers, SSNs)
Document fingerprinting — Identifying specific documents
Statistical analysis — Detecting anomalous data movements

blocks.text: DLP is most effective when combined with proper data classification. Without classification, DLP cannot reliably identify what data needs protection. ⚠️ Exam Trap: DLP requires data classification to work effectively. If data isn't classified, DLP has no way to know what's sensitive.

items: At Rest — Full-disk encryption (FDE), file-level encryption, database encryption
In Transit — TLS, IPsec, VPN, S/MIME for email
In Use — Homomorphic encryption, secure enclaves (emerging technology)
Encryption does NOT replace access controls — use both
Key management is critical — lost keys = lost data

blocks.text: Encryption is one of the most important data security controls across all data states:
From the Official CBK: Email content protection example — "Private: Email and attachments must be encrypted with AES 256." Key Management Considerations:

items: Who creates keys?
How are keys stored and protected?
How are keys distributed?
When are keys rotated?
How are keys revoked/destroyed?
What happens if a key is compromised?
Access should follow need-to-know and least privilege principles
Mandatory Access Control (MAC) — System-enforced based on labels/clearances
Discretionary Access Control (DAC) — Owner decides who can access
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) — Access based on job role/function
Access must be reviewed regularly (access reviews/recertification)

blocks.text: From Shon Harris: "In MAC, the system compares the subject's security clearance to the object's security label. In DAC, the system compares the subject's identity to the ACL on the resource." ⚠️ Exam Trap: MAC is the MOST restrictive model — the system enforces access based on labels, and even the data owner cannot override these restrictions. DAC is the LEAST restrictive — the owner has full control over who accesses their data.
Digital Rights Management (DRM) and Information Rights Management (IRM)

items: DRM — technologies that control how digital content (music, video, software, e-books) is used, copied, and distributed
IRM — applies DRM concepts to enterprise documents and email (e.g., preventing forwarding, printing, or copying of sensitive documents)
DRM/IRM enforces persistent protection — controls travel with the data regardless of location
Common DRM techniques: licensing, encryption, digital watermarking, online authentication, automatic expiration
DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act) — prohibits circumvention of DRM/copyright protection mechanisms

blocks.text: From Destination CISSP: "The purpose of DRM is to prevent the unauthorized use, modification, and distribution of copyrighted works such as intellectual property." DRM techniques include:

items: Licensing — grants access and defines terms of use; tied to specific devices or accounts
Encryption — content is encrypted; only authorized users with valid licenses can decrypt
Digital watermarking — embedded tags that tie content to specific license holders for tracking unauthorized distribution
Persistent online authentication — requires periodic connection to verify license validity
Automatic expiration — content access expires after a defined period

blocks.text: IRM extends DRM to enterprise environments. Examples:

items: Microsoft Azure Information Protection / Purview — prevent email forwarding, restrict document printing
Adobe Document Cloud — persistent PDF access controls
Enterprise IRM can restrict: copying, printing, screen capture, forwarding, editing

blocks.text: From Chapple: "Persistent online authentication, automatic expiration, and a continuous audit trail are all methods used with digital rights management (DRM) technologies." ⚠️ Exam Trap: DRM protects copyrighted content (music, video, software). IRM protects enterprise data (documents, email). Both provide persistent protection that follows the data. The exam may test the distinction between DRM and IRM, or ask about DMCA provisions that make circumventing DRM illegal.
